title: New gas power policy of China’s Guangdong province drives structural shift from baseload to peak-only dispatch
gist: Guangdong's July 2025 reform replaced guaranteed dispatch hours and gas-cost subsidies for gas-fired power with pure economic dispatch plus capacity payments that cover full capex, pushing the province's 61 GW gas fleet from baseload into peak-only operation. Because Guangdong is ~one-third of China's gas power capacity and 28% of national LNG demand, and other provinces are copying the framework, Wood Mackenzie sees a structural downgrade to Chinese power-sector gas demand growth — with coal-to-gas switching only economic below roughly US$6/mmbtu spot LNG.

insights.claim: Guangdong province accounts for roughly one-third of China's total gas power capacity and 10% of national GDP, making its dispatch rules a leading indicator for the direction of China's gas and LNG market.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Track Guangdong policy filings as the highest-signal proxy for Chinese LNG offtake trends rather than waiting for national-level statistics.
insights.quote: Guangdong accounts for 10% of China's GDP and around one-third of the country's total gas power capacity.
insights.locator: Guangdong accounts for 10% of China's GDP

insights.claim: In 2025 Guangdong consumed 41 bcm of gas and 18 Mt of LNG, equal to 10% and 28% of China's national totals respectively — meaning the province is far more LNG-intensive than its share of overall gas consumption.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Any demand destruction in Guangdong hits seaborne LNG nearly three times harder than it hits total Chinese gas demand, concentrating the risk on LNG suppliers and spot cargo flows.
insights.quote: In 2025, Guangdong consumed 41 bcm of gas and had LNG demand of 18 Mt, representing 10% and 28% of the national totals, respectively.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie is branding the province's adaptation as the "Guangdong Model", a template it expects other Chinese provinces to follow in repositioning gas fleets within a high-renewable grid.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: If the model propagates, LNG demand forecasts built on Chinese gas-fired baseload assumptions need to be re-based downward province by province.
insights.quote: highlighting the "Guangdong Model" as a guide for how China's largest gas power market is adapting to a high-renewable grid
insights.locator: Kai Dong, Principal Analyst for Asia Pacific Gas

insights.claim: Guangdong's solar and wind capacity rose from 14 GW to 105 GW between 2020 and 2026, a roughly eightfold increase that created the need for flexible dispatchable balancing capacity.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The speed of the renewables ramp — not policy ideology — is what compressed thermal running hours; expect the same sequencing wherever provincial solar builds accelerate.
insights.quote: Solar and wind capacity in Guangdong increased from 14 GW to 105 GW between 2020 and 2026
insights.locator: Renewables surge forces gas into a new role

insights.claim: Gas-fired capacity in Guangdong more than doubled from 27 GW to 61 GW between 2020 and 2026, so falling utilisation is happening on a much larger installed base rather than a shrinking one.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Turbine OEMs and EPC contractors can still see volume growth in China even as gas molecules demand growth slows — capacity and fuel demand have decoupled.
insights.quote: Gas power capacity more than doubled in response, rising from 27 GW to 61 GW over the same period.
insights.locator: Renewables surge forces gas into a new role

insights.claim: Coal and nuclear capacity in Guangdong grew more slowly than gas and renewables over 2020-2026 and continue to carry baseload duty, leaving gas as the marginal system regulator rather than a baseload competitor to coal.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Coal's baseload position in southern China is more defensible than gas-switching narratives imply, supporting thermal coal demand resilience.
insights.quote: Coal and nuclear grew more slowly, supporting baseload demand.
insights.locator: Coal and nuclear grew more slowly

insights.claim: Gas fleets can successfully reposition themselves as system regulators in a grid with rapidly rising renewables, rather than being stranded by intermittent generation.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The equity risk for Chinese gas generators is margin mix (capacity vs energy revenue), not asset stranding — value accrues to availability, not throughput.
insights.quote: Guangdong's experience tells us that gas power fleets can successfully reposition themselves in the grid of increasing renewables
insights.locator: Between 2020 and 2026, gas-fired capacity more than doubled

insights.claim: Guangdong's July 2025 gas power reform abolished the previous regime of guaranteed dispatch hours, an approved on-grid tariff, and a subsidy triggered when the system-wide weighted average cost of gas exceeded a threshold.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Removal of the WACOG-linked subsidy strips out the mechanism that previously insulated Chinese gas generators from high LNG prices — fuel-price pass-through risk now sits with the plant.
insights.quote: Gas plants previously operated with guaranteed dispatch hours, an approved on-grid tariff, and additional subsidy when system-wide weighted average cost of gas (WACOG) is beyond certain level.
insights.locator: New policy: from guaranteed hours to pure economic dispatch

insights.claim: Under the new framework gas plants must bid into pure economic dispatch to recover their fuel costs, so generation volumes are now set by spot fuel economics rather than administrative allocation.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Chinese gas-fired output becomes price-elastic to LNG — expect Guangdong gas burn to swing with the JKM curve instead of being locked in.
insights.quote: The new policy introduces pure economic dispatch, requiring plants to bid to recover fuel costs
insights.locator: New policy: from guaranteed hours to pure economic dispatch

insights.claim: Capacity payments in Guangdong have been raised to cover full capital expenditure instead of only partial recovery, compensating plants for availability rather than for generation.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Cash flows for Chinese gas IPPs shift toward regulated, volume-independent capacity revenue — a de-risked but capped return profile that changes how these assets should be valued.
insights.quote: capacity payments have increased significantly, now covering full capital expenditure instead of only partial recovery
insights.locator: In exchange, capacity payments have increased

insights.claim: Paying for availability rather than output is itself the mechanism that locks gas plants into a peaking role, because operators no longer need running hours to earn a return on capital.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Capacity-market design, not fuel price alone, is the lever that determines Chinese gas burn — watch other provinces' capacity payment levels as the forward indicator.
insights.quote: The policy compensates plants for availability rather than generation, reinforcing the shift to peaking roles.
insights.locator: In exchange, capacity payments have increased

insights.claim: Spot LNG prices must fall to roughly US$6/mmbtu — after taxes, regasification and pipeline tariffs — before efficient gas power fleets can economically displace subcritical coal plants at a US$95/ton coal price.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A hard, tradeable switching level: sustained spot LNG below ~$6/mmbtu unlocks a step-change in Chinese gas burn; above it, incremental demand stays capped.
insights.quote: spot LNG prices must fall to about US$6/mmbtu before efficient gas power fleets can economically replace subcritical coal plants based on a US$95/ton coal price

insights.claim: The switching economics are quoted net of taxes, regasification and pipeline tariffs, meaning the delivered-cost stack — not the headline cargo price — is what gates Chinese coal-to-gas substitution.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Midstream tariff reform in China would move the switching threshold as much as a fall in cargo prices — a second, less-watched lever on LNG demand.
insights.quote: after accounting for taxes, regasification, and pipeline tariffs

insights.claim: Until spot LNG reaches the switching threshold, most Guangdong gas fleets are expected to remain primarily in peaking roles, limiting their contribution to total power-sector gas demand.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Do not model Chinese power gas demand off installed gas capacity growth — utilisation, not megawatts, is the binding variable.
insights.quote: most fleets are likely to remain primarily in peaking roles., restricting their impact on total power gas demand
insights.locator: Until then, most fleets are likely

themes.theme: Structural downside to LNG demand growth

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie forecasts that a shift to peak-only dispatch will slow the growth of China's power-sector gas demand relative to a scenario where plants maintained baseload operations.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A downgrade to the single largest assumed source of incremental global LNG demand — bearish for long-dated LNG contracting and new liquefaction FIDs.
insights.quote: Wood Mackenzie forecasts that shifting to peak-only dispatch will slow the growth of China’s power gas demand compared to maintaining baseload operations.
insights.locator: National replication creates a structural downside

insights.claim: With other Chinese provinces adopting a similar dispatch framework, the open question for the global LNG market is how much less demand growth this implies versus prior expectations — an explicit flag that consensus LNG forecasts may be too high.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Positions the analyst against bullish Chinese LNG demand consensus; watch for forecast revisions from IEA, Shell and Wood Mackenzie itself as provincial replication is confirmed.
insights.quote: With China’s other provinces following similar framework, the key question for the global LNG market is how much less demand growth this could mean than previously anticipated.
insights.locator: With China’s other provinces following similar framework

insights.claim: Chinese gas-fired power capacity will keep growing to support grid stability in a high-renewable system even as plants run fewer hours, decoupling capacity additions from fuel demand.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Headlines about Chinese gas plant approvals are a false positive for LNG bulls — capacity growth no longer translates into proportional gas burn.
insights.quote: The policy shift means plants will run fewer hours, and that distinction matters enormously for China’s gas market.
insights.locator: Gas-fired power capacity in China will continue to grow
